idiom_name: java.lang.ref.WeakReference plus ReferenceQueue; WeakHashMap; SoftReference for caches; Cleaner for post-mortem work
implementation_notes: Java has carried the reference-object facility in its core library since 1.2: a WeakReference holds a referent the collector may clear, get() returns null after clearing, and registering the reference with a ReferenceQueue is how a structure learns that its entry died - WeakHashMap simply polls its queue on every access instead of running a thread. The package summary assigns the strengths: weak references for canonicalizing mappings that must not prevent their keys or values from being reclaimed, soft references for memory-sensitive caches, phantom references and Cleaner for post-mortem cleanup (the documented replacement for finalize). Hand-written registries therefore collapse into the provided containers, and the remaining discipline is the promotion: read get() once into a local and check it.
pitfalls: WeakHashMap keys are compared with equals/hashCode, not identity: equal-but-distinct keys collapse into one entry, and a key whose value refers back to it keeps the entry alive forever.

Clearing only happens when the collector notices; without a ReferenceQueue - and someone to drain it - stale entries accumulate, and the class documents that size() can shrink as if another thread were silently removing entries.

SoftReference is a memory-pressure hint rather than an eviction contract (the JVM may clear it aggressively on dynamic heaps), so caches still need their own policy; the same is true of WeakHashMap as a cache.
A reference is enqueued only if the reference object itself stays strongly reachable - dropping the WeakReference, or storing it weakly, silently cancels the notification.
